Empirical Research Plan: Schooling Returns Using Monozygotic-Twin Differences

============================================================

1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Within–monozygotic-twin fixed effects (sibling-difference design) combined with an errors-in-variables instrumental-variables (IV) correction that uses the co-twin’s independent report of schooling as an instrument for each twin’s self-reported schooling.  

Why it fits:  
• MZ twins share genes and family background → differencing within pairs removes those unobservables.  
• Self-reported schooling is noisy; a second, independent report delivers a classical-type instrument that is correlated with true schooling but, conditional on true schooling and shared background, uncorrelated with the individual-specific wage shock.  
• Neither DID, RDD, nor event-study frameworks exploit the key feature here—paired individuals with known genetic identity—so a sibling FE/IV design is the natural choice.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: Years of completed schooling (continuous). In pair-difference form, treatment = (Twin A years of school – Twin B years of school).  
Control group / counterfactual: The lower-schooling co-twin serves as the counterfactual for the higher-schooling twin; with FE, each pair supplies its own control.  
Timing / event date: Not applicable—schooling completed prior to observed wages.  
Running variable & cutoff: Not applicable.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1 (Shared-factor elimination): After conditioning on pair fixed effects, all genetic and family-background influences on wages are purged. Plausible for MZ twins reared together.  
A2 (Within-pair exogeneity): The idiosyncratic factors that drive one twin to obtain more education are uncorrelated with twin-specific wage shocks. Potentially violated if, e.g., health shocks both reduce schooling and earnings; we mitigate with controls and robustness checks.  
A3 (Instrument relevance): The co-twin’s report is strongly correlated with true schooling. Plausible; measurement-error studies show >0.8 correlation. Testable with first-stage F-stat.  
A4 (Instrument exclusion): Conditional on own true schooling and pair FE, the co-twin’s report affects own wages only through its correlation with true schooling (i.e., no direct effect). Plausible because it is merely a report, not an action, and the respondent does not observe it at the time of labor-market decisions.  
A5 (SUTVA within pairs): One twin’s schooling affects only that twin’s wage (no spillovers). Could fail if twins share jobs or firms; we test by dropping pairs who report working together.  

4. Main Threats and Responses  
T1 Non-shared omitted factors (health shocks, local labor demand) → add controls (age, sex, race, marital status, union status, tenure) and test sensitivity to adding self-reported childhood health.  
T2 Measurement error in both schooling reports → use both cross-reports as instruments (over-identification) or structural errors-in-variables estimator; perform Hansen J-test.  
T3 Sample selection (festival volunteers may be unusual) → re-weight to CPS schooling/earnings margins; compare main estimates to CPS-based sibling-difference estimates as an external validity check.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -----------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
# -----------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data I/O
library(fixest)       # FE and IV regressions
library(modelsummary) # regression tables

# -----------------------------------------
# 1. Load and inspect data
# -----------------------------------------
df <- fread("twins_festival.csv")  # Assume long format: one row per twin

# -----------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# -----------------------------------------
# unique pair id must exist, call it pair_id; twin_id identifies the individual
df[, ln_wage  := log(hourly_wage)]
# Center variables by pair to create differences automatically in FE spec
# Create instruments: co-twin’s report of my schooling
setorder(df, pair_id, twin_id)     # ensure order
df[, cotwin_report := shift(report_schooling, type = "lead"), by = pair_id]
df[is.na(cotwin_report), cotwin_report := shift(report_schooling, type = "lag"), by = pair_id]

# -----------------------------------------
# 3. Main specifications
# -----------------------------------------
# 3.1 OLS with controls
ols <- feols(ln_wage ~ self_schooling + age + I(age^2) + race + sex + marital + union + tenure, data=df)

# 3.2 Monozygotic-twin fixed effects (within-pair)
fe <- feols(ln_wage ~ self_schooling + age + I(age^2) + race + sex + marital + union + tenure | pair_id, data=df)

# 3.3 FE‐IV correcting for measurement error
fe_iv <- feols(ln_wage ~ 1 | pair_id | self_schooling ~ cotwin_report,
               data=df,
               vcov = "cluster")

# -----------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness: Drop pairs working in same firm
# -----------------------------------------
fe_iv_rb <- feols(ln_wage ~ 1 | pair_id | self_schooling ~ cotwin_report,
                  data=df[shared_employer==0],
                  vcov = "cluster")

# -----------------------------------------
# 5. Present results
# -----------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(OLS=ols, TwinFE=fe, FE_IV=fe_iv, FE_IV_NoSameFirm=fe_iv_rb),
             statistic = "({stat})",
             stars = TRUE)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory and prior U.S. studies suggest a 5–10 percent log-wage return per additional year of schooling. Twin-difference designs typically bring this down slightly; correcting for measurement error nudges it back up.  
Prior: β ≈ 0.06 (≈ 6 percent) in the FE-IV estimate.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = yes, 0 = questionable)  
C1 Sufficient within-pair variation in schooling: 1  
C2 Exogeneity of within-pair schooling differences: 0.5 (some concern about health shocks)  
C3 Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10): 1  
C4 Instrument exclusion (only affects wages through schooling): 0.5  
C5 No spillovers / SUTVA within pairs: 0.5  

Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 → reasonable but warrants robustness and sensitivity analyses.
